meta.title: Who really said "We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — JFK said it at Rice University on 12 September 1962. The speech was drafted by Ted Sorensen; the exact wording and fuller context are verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: John F. Kennedy spoke the line at Rice University, 12 Sept 1962, in a speech drafted by Ted Sorensen. See the primary source and full context.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Kennedy delivered this line in his “Address at Rice University on the Nation’s Space Effort” at Rice Stadium in Houston on 12 September 1962. The event was recorded, filmed, and transcribed, and the wording is confirmed against the archival text held by the JFK Presidential Library ↗.

source.heading: The primary source

docMeta.dd: Address at Rice University on the Nation’s Space Effort
Theodore “Ted” Sorensen, with edits by Kennedy

source.excerpt: But why, some say, the Moon? Why choose this as our goal? … We choose to go to the Moon. We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard; because that goal will serve to organize and measure the best of our energies and skills, because that challenge is one that we are willing to accept, one we are unwilling to postpone, and one we intend to win, and the others, too.
trail: The full authenticated transcript is published by Rice University ↗, host of the 1962 address.
Wikipedia ↗ documents the date, venue, and Ted Sorensen’s authorship of the drafts.
Rice News ↗ notes the speech was typed by Sorensen and that Kennedy jotted the ‘Why does Rice play Texas?’ line between the lines.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version usually stops at ‘hard’ and drops ‘and do the other things’
source.excerptNote: Immediately before this passage Kennedy ad-libbed the crowd-pleasing line “Why does Rice play Texas?” — a jibe he had added by hand to Sorensen’s typed draft.

author.name: John F. Kennedy
author.heading: John F. Kennedy
author.bio: John Fitzgerald Kennedy served as the 35th U.S. President from 1961 until his assassination in November 1963. In 1961 he set the national goal of a crewed Moon landing before the decade’s end, and his 1962 Rice University address became the defining public statement of that ambition. As with most presidential oratory, the text was principally drafted by his counsel and speechwriter Ted Sorensen, then shaped and delivered by Kennedy.

misattribution.heading: How it gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Kennedy is correct — the recurring errors are about the wording and the author behind the President, not the speaker.

items.who: “…not because it is easy, but because it is hard”
items.why: The clipped popular version drops “and do the other things” and singularises the pronouns. The authenticated transcript ↗ reads “…not because they are easy, but because they are hard.”

Sorensen drafted the speech and deserves real credit, but the words were delivered as Kennedy’s own after Kennedy’s edits, per the record ↗. Convention rightly attributes the spoken line to the President.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the line is genuinely John F. Kennedy’s, spoken at Rice University on 12 September 1962 — drafted by Sorensen — and is most accurately quoted with “and do the other things” and the plural “they are hard,” per the Rice University transcript ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Kennedy spoke roughly a year after committing the nation, before Congress, to landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out. The Rice address was the public, rhetorical case for a program that at its peak consumed a large share of the federal budget.

The “not because they are easy, but because they are hard” construction reframed difficulty itself as the reason for the endeavour — a rhetorical inversion that has since been borrowed for countless ambitious goals far beyond spaceflight.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the ‘Rice play Texas’ line
detailsBody: Just before the famous sentence, Kennedy delivered the aside “Why does Rice play Texas?” — a nod to the local college-football rivalry that he had added in his own hand to Sorensen’s typed draft. It drew a roar from the Houston crowd and is preserved in the recording of the speech.
